name: High-protein diet
lead: A high-protein diet emphasizes protein-rich foods such as meat, fish, eggs, dairy and legumes. Definitions vary: Wikipedia describes it as drawing 40 percent or more of daily calories from protein, while other sources use thresholds above the US recommended dietary allowance of 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight per day, or around 1.2 to 2.0 g/kg for active people.[1][2]

Within looksmaxxing communities, protein is discussed for building muscle, staying full while cutting, and supporting hair, skin and other tissues; a recent social-media trend called "protein maxxing" focuses on maximizing intake.[2] Research links higher protein intake to greater muscle mass and less muscle loss during energy deficits, while reviews disagree on kidney and cardiovascular risks.[1]

paras: Many commercial high-protein diets, including Atkins and Protein Power, also restrict carbohydrates, and Wikipedia notes that some are high in saturated fat.[1] Atkins' Diet Revolution was published in 1972 by cardiologist Robert Atkins.[2]

Higher protein intake is associated with greater muscle mass, better gains from resistance training and less muscle loss during energy deficits, according to a 2018 meta-analysis and a 2019 review cited by Wikipedia.[1] Mechanisms proposed include greater satiety through hormones such as GLP-1, CCK and PYY, and a higher thermic effect of protein.[2]

A 2005 trial reported that a high-protein diet sustained reductions in appetite, calorie intake and body weight despite compensatory hormone changes.[3] A 2010 NEJM trial examined diets with high or low protein content and glycemic index for weight-loss maintenance.[4]

Trials of higher-protein diets have measured weight, fat mass and fat-free mass, including the 2005 appetite study and the 2010 weight-maintenance trial noted above.[3][4][5] A 2013 meta-analysis compared dietary approaches for type 2 diabetes.[5] A 2020 meta-analysis found no significant improvement in blood pressure or glycemic control among people with type 2 diabetes.[1] No controlled trials were found that test high protein intake for hair, skin or facial appearance.

A 2017 review suggested intake above 1.5 g/kg of ideal body weight may contribute to kidney damage, whereas a 2023 umbrella review found no evidence that intake above 0.8 g/kg/day specifically triggers chronic kidney disease.[1] The American Heart Association has said diets high in protein and saturated fat raise risk of coronary artery disease and cancer, and its 2001 committee recommended against some high-protein diets citing a lack of long-term studies.[1]

Reported effects of restrictive versions include constipation, headaches and bad breath, particularly with low fiber intake.[2] People with kidney, liver or diabetic conditions are advised to consult clinicians.[2]

timeline.event: AHA Nutrition Committee advises against some high-protein diets.[1]

lore.intro: Forum users debate how much protein is useful beyond muscle building.[6]

claims.claim: Very high protein intake improves hair, skin, collagen and other tissues beyond muscle.
claims.believers: One looksmax.org poster asked whether mass amounts of protein could support hair, collagen, the nervous system and bones depleted by lifting, while replies suggested little marginal benefit beyond about 1 g per pound.[6]
claims.experts: No published trials were found testing very high protein intake for hair, skin or facial appearance; kidney effects at high intakes are debated.[1]

card.summary: Protein-forward eating for muscle retention and fullness; supported for those goals, untested for hair or skin claims.
card.note: Kidney effects at very high intakes are debated; people with kidney disease are advised to consult clinicians.

quick.overview:
A high-protein diet raises protein above the standard 0.8 g/kg recommended allowance, usually through meat, fish, eggs, dairy and legumes. It is popular for cutting and muscle building.

Higher intake is linked to more muscle and less muscle loss during energy deficits; claims about hair or skin have not been tested.
quick.mechanism: Protein increases satiety, has a higher thermic effect than carbohydrates or fat, and supplies amino acids for muscle repair.
quick.risks: Reviews disagree on kidney risk at higher intakes. Restrictive versions may cause constipation, headaches or bad breath, and the AHA has cautioned about diets high in saturated fat.
